cues.text: In this town,
we had to freeze whenever the bell rang.
Nobody would tell me who rang it.
Nobody would explain the scraping noise just before it.
And last week, my neighbor moved before the second ring.
His house had been empty since.
At school, we practiced standing still with bread on our heads.
My best friend always ate his before the lesson ended.
At the market, the baker kept her loaves in low piles.
We scratched our noses before carrying anything heavy.
We froze with baskets halfway to the counter.
We kept our heads down, even when shadows crossed the square.
After the next ring, the whole market started again.
Our golem kept looking down, even after the second ring.
My neighbor used to save me the biggest bun.
Even with the bell, I liked living there.
But that empty house kept bringing back one question.
Who rang the bell?
Whenever I asked, the adults warned me away from the tower.
One wrong tug could stop the whole town.
They wouldn't even let me near the rope.
So I watched it from across the square.
One afternoon, I saw it twitch by itself.
It ran through a tiny hole in the town wall.
The scraping started on the other side.
Then the bell rang, and a shadow crossed my shoes.
I kept my head down.
I asked the oldest woman what was behind that wall.
She looked at my neighbor's empty doorstep.
She brushed dust from her doorstep for a moment. Then she said, "Don't move until the second ring."
She shut her door.
That night, I lay perfectly still in bed. What did we look like when none of us moved?
I wanted to see whoever was pulling that rope.
First, I piled hay bales beside the wall.
From up there, I thought I could see over it.
I was one bale short when the whole pile leaned.
My friend found me with only my shoes sticking out.
Everyone laughed. I was still spitting out hay.
After that, I spent my evenings behind the tower.
This time, I followed the rope.
Behind some loose boards, I found a gap through the wall.
I wedged them apart, a little more each night.
By Friday, I could squeeze through without touching the rope.
But I had only tried the gap after dark.
I needed to be there when the bell rang.
If I got stuck, nobody could move to help.
My neighbor's door was still shut.
I packed water, a little torch, some rope, bread, and one extra bun wrapped in a clean cloth.
My neighbor always gave me the bigger one.
My best friend caught me packing before school.
"What if you don't come back?" he asked.
"Then keep a bun for me," I said.
He didn't laugh this time.
The next morning, the boards felt cold against my hands.
Above me, the rope disappeared into the dark.
I looked back through the gap between the houses.
The baker was stacking loaves in her low piles.
My friend was eating his lesson again.
And beside them, my neighbor's stool was empty.
I pulled both straps tight against my shoulders. Then I bent my knees and took one steady breath.
Then the scraping started, right above my head.
The first ring shook the boards beside me.
My feet stopped before I could think.
Then I made myself crawl through.
The gap pressed my bag against my back.
Beside my face, the rope jerked upward.
A thin strip of light opened over my head,
and the ground outside was smooth, cold wood.
I crouched behind the wall and waited for the scraping to stop.
The smell of warm bread had gone.
Something nearby breathed through its nose.
I climbed onto a screw and looked over the edge.
Our town was in a toy box.
A boy was holding the lid.
The lid pulled the rope and rang our bell.
It rang again as he shut it.
We had been pretending to be toys.
My neighbor was under a jar beside the box.
He was still alive.
I held up his bun.
Then I reached for the glass,
and a shadow covered my hand.
Then I remembered the golem.
He never looked up, even when the bell was quiet.
So I looked up.
And I saw...
